title: Decision log: small-LLM approximation and SLO tradeoffs
content:
Purpose and scope:
- Quick decision log for a current customer POC (financial SaaS) focused on sub-150ms p50 on 8-token responses and sub-400ms p95 for conversational turn completions.
- Goal: enumerate small-LLM approximations (lighter models / quantized variants) + routing strategies to hit latency SLOs with acceptable quality regression and cost targets.
- Audience: SEs running experiments, infra engineers validating configs, solutions PM.

Context / constraints:
- Customer workload: mix of short chat (few-shot instructions + retrieval snippets) and a small subset of longer-generation tasks (summaries). 60% of requests are <= 128 input tokens.
- Deployment modes for the POC: Redwood Dedicated pool (8x A100-ish equiv) with potential edge-burst to hosted endpoints.
- Latency SLOs: p50 <= 150ms for short responses, p95 <= 400ms. Budget constraint: target < 60% of the naive baseline per-token GPU cost.
- Quality guardrails: top-line acceptance metric is pairwise preference vs baseline Llama2-13B at >= 85% on customer prompt set (10k examples sampled).

Model candidates considered (selection rationale):
- M1: Mistral-7B-Instruct (dense) — good instruction-tuned behavior, small memory footprint, strong latency baseline.
- M2: Llama-2-13B -> quantized int8/GPTQ -> serves as quality baseline but heavier; useful as fallback.
- M3: Falcon-7B-Compressed (GPTQ) — aggressive compaction, good throughput on tensor cores with fused kernels.
- M4: OpenMini-3B distilled variant (customer-provided research model) — minimal mem, unknown worst-case hallucination profile.
- M5: 7B-chat-quant-int4 candidate (experimental GPTQ chain) — lowest memory, highest risk.

Quantization options and tradeoffs (current thinking):
- fp16 baseline: highest quality, highest memory and cost. Use only for fallbacks (pinned sessions) and for a/b quality checks.
- int8 (bnb): typically ~1.5-2x memory reduction vs fp16; minimal quality impact for most LLMs. Good default for Dedicated.
- GPTQ 4-bit (W8A8->W4A16 style): ~3-4x mem reduction, occasional token-level artifacts; needs per-model calibration and evals. Good candidate for latency-first routing.
- int4 (experimental) via llama.cpp style: fastest on CPU edge, but we don't have CPU-edge in the POC yet. Flag for later.

Inference kernel / runtime notes:
- Exllama / llama-cuda / TRTexec: test throughput and memory tradeoffs across the same quantized artifact. Kernel choice shifts latency tail behavior significantly.
- Continuous batching: target dynamic batching but cap max batch window at 6ms to preserve latency SLO. Test both synchronous and async batching.
- KV cache pinning: for chat scenarios, keep warm KV caches for active sessions (can save 20-40% per-token work). Include TTL heuristics.

Routing strategy ideas (latency-led):
- Fast-pass: route short requests (<=128 tokens) to quantized 7B (M1 or M3) with aggressive batching and int8/GPTQ profile.
- Quality-fallback: if final score/heuristic indicates low-confidence (entropy threshold, generation length over threshold, or safety classifier), route to baseline 13B fp16 with higher cost.
- Canary A/B: maintain 5% traffic to a mid-tier 13B quantized instance to monitor regressions via automatic pairwise evals.
- Region fallback: prioritize routing to local region Dedicated; if capacity limited, fall back to hosted API variant in adjacent region tuned to same prompt pipeline.

Prompt / pipeline modifications to reduce compute without losing quality:
- Prefix pruning: move heavy context (long docs) into retrieved context embeddings and include only top-3 passages (instead of full 10). Test MRR and nDCG impact.
- Decompose long tasks: if user asks for multi-step summarization, return short actionable bullet summary first (fast path) and queue a full summary via async job (delayed).
- Reranker + smaller generator: use small 3B model to produce candidate rewrites, then rerank with a faster embedding-similarity check before invoking larger model. Saves generator invocations.
- System messages: centralize system-level instructions to fixed prompt stored in KV cache to avoid re-sending large system prompts every request.

Planned experiments (priority order):
1) Baseline baseline: measure p50/p95/tokens_per_second for: M2 fp16 (13B baseline), M1 int8 (Mistral-7B), M3 GPTQ (Falcon-7B). Record memory and cost per 1M tokens.
2) Cache + small-batch: enable KV cache warm-start for repeated sessions and test steady-state latency reduction.
3) GPTQ quality sweep: run 2000-customer prompts across int8 vs GPTQ-4bit variants and compute pairwise preference and token-level error modes.
4) Routing sim: offline simulation of routing heuristics using historical trace (sample of 50k requests) to estimate cost and missed-quality events.
5) Prompt-shortening ablation: compare full context vs top-3 passages vs top-1 passage for retrieval hits; monitor F1 on extraction tasks.

Metrics and logging to capture:
- Latency: p50, p90, p95 end-to-end (client-to-client), and server-only generation time.
- Quality: pairwise preference vs baseline, BLEU/ROUGE where appropriate, hallucination rate (manual sampling), safety classifier flags.
- Cost: GPU token cost, tokens-per-dollar, active sessions memory footprint.
- Routing correctness: false-positive fallback rates, fallback latency delta.
- Operational: model-load times, cold-start penalties, GPU utilization, OOM incidents.

Recommended default POC config (starter):
- Primary model: M1 (Mistral-7B-Instruct) int8 with exllama kernels.
- Fallback: Llama-2-13B quant int8 fp16 when available; full fp16 for offline batch QA.
- Batching: dynamic batching 1-8 with 6ms max coalescing window.
- Caching: session KV cache TTL 15 minutes for interactive sessions.
- Routing: fast-pass to primary; fallback to 13B if generation length > 256 tokens or entropy > 0.85.

Open questions / risks (to resolve during POC):
- Customer acceptance threshold: is pairwise preference vs 13B at 85% sufficient or do they want 90%? Ask customer in next sync. (Owner: Priya)
- GPTQ artifacts: do we have tooling to detect token-level truncation / decoding glitches automatically? Need small auto-detector (JIRA-10872).
- Kernel availability: exllama + TRT binary compatibility with our Dedicated runtime kernels — some ops fail on older driver stacks. Need infra runbook (Owner: Daniel).
- Regulatory logging: if routing to hosted fallback, ensure audit trail does not leak PII — need privacy review (Owner: Marco).

Next steps (short-term milestones):
- Week 0-1: run baseline latency and cost benchmarks for selected candidates (Ava / Daniel).
- Week 1-2: run GPTQ vs int8 quality sweep and produce pairwise preference matrix (Priya / Marco).
- Week 2: simulate routing decisions against historical trace and produce recommended thresholds (SE team).
- Week 3: prepare a customer-facing one-pager with recommended config and observable SLA dashboard spec (Ava).

Notes to self / rough todo checklist:
- [ ] Upload trace subset to experiment bucket and anonymize.
- [ ] Add eval harness to GitHub PR referenced above and wire results to Confluence summary.
- [ ] Test model-load times on Dedicated nodes with 4 concurrent warm sessions.
- [ ] Draft fallback privacy checklist for hosted fallbacks.

References and links:
- Confluence experiment spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=8342103
- JIRA ticket tracking GPTQ detection: JIRA-10872
- Experiment PR: github.com/redwood-inference/poc-experiments/pull/47

Quick decision (this doc):
- Proceed with Mistral-7B int8 as the fast-path primary and use Llama-2-13B quantized as the safety fallback. Prioritize a GPTQ quality sweep but do not flip to 4-bit production until automated artifact detection exists and the customer accepts up to 15% quality regression vs baseline.

Unresolved: customer final quality threshold and hosted-fallback privacy checklist completion.
